sections.title: 4 Methodology
sections.text: 4 Methodology We introduce Safety Optimal Transport (SOT), which reformulates safe fine-tuning as a distribution level alignment task. As shown in Fig. 1 , SOT includes two stages: dual-reference distributional weight learning and safety-aware fine-tuning. 4.1 Dual-Reference Distributional Weight Learning The core objective of SOT is to learn a global weight vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}] 𝐰 \mathbf{w} that assigns importance to each instance in the downstream dataset [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}_{\text{custom}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{c}}] 𝒟 custom = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 N c \mathcal{D}_{\text{custom}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{c}} . Rather than treating data selection as a collection of independent binary decisions that often fails to capture collective semantic relationships, we reformulate the problem as learning a continuous probability measure. Specifically, we represent the weighted dataset as a discrete empirical distribution [LaTeX: P(\mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{c}}w_{i}\delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})},] P ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) = ∑ i = 1 N c w i ​ δ ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 i ) , P(\mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{c}}w_{i}\delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})}, (3) where weight vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}\in\Delta^{N_{c}-1}] 𝐰 ∈ Δ N c − 1 \mathbf{w}\in\Delta^{N_{c}-1} satisfies [LaTeX: \sum w_{i}=1] ∑ w i = 1 \sum w_{i}=1 and [LaTeX: w_{i}\geq 0] w i ≥ 0 w_{i}\geq 0 , and [LaTeX: \delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})}] δ ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 i ) \delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})} denotes the Dirac mass at location [LaTeX: (\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})] ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 i ) (\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i}) . Optimizing [LaTeX: P(\mathbf{w})] P ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) P(\mathbf{w}) requires explicit geometric guidance, we design a dual-reference strategy. (1) Task-Specific Alignment (Pull): The distribution [LaTeX: P(\mathbf{w})] P ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) P(\mathbf{w}) must align with trusted data from the target domain to preserve downstream utility while ensuring safety. We construct a distribution [LaTeX: Q] Q Q using a small, verified subset [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}] 𝒟 safe \mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} (e.g., a few dozen samples) sampled from the downstream task distribution, which acts as a high-precision anchor to ensure the learned weights prioritize samples that are both safe and utility-preserving. (2) General Harm Repulsion (Push): The distribution [LaTeX: P(\mathbf{w})] P ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) P(\mathbf{w}) must actively maximize its distance from broad toxicity patterns to establish a robust geometric safety margin. We employ a subset of a publicly available harmful dataset [LaTeX: \mathcal{D_{\text{harmful}}}] 𝒟 harmful \mathcal{D_{\text{harmful}}} (e.g., red-teaming benchmarks) to represent generic toxicity patterns and build the distribution [LaTeX: M] M M , which serves as a repulsive source without requiring domain-specific harmful data collection. Both references are formulated as uniform distributions: [LaTeX: Q=\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}\frac{1}{N_{s}}\delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{y}_{j})^{s}},M=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{h}}\frac{1}{N_{h}}\delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{k},\mathbf{y}_{k})^{h}},] Q = ∑ j = 1 N s 1 N s ​ δ ( 𝐱 j , 𝐲 j ) s , M = ∑ k = 1 N h 1 N h ​ δ ( 𝐱 k , 𝐲 k ) h , Q=\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}\frac{1}{N_{s}}\delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{y}_{j})^{s}},M=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{h}}\frac{1}{N_{h}}\delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{k},\mathbf{y}_{k})^{h}}, (4) where each [LaTeX: (\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{y}_{j})^{\text{s}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}] ( 𝐱 j , 𝐲 j ) s ∼ 𝒟 safe (\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{y}_{j})^{\text{s}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} and [LaTeX: (\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{y}_{j})^{\text{h}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}}] ( 𝐱 j , 𝐲 j ) h ∼ 𝒟 harmful (\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{y}_{j})^{\text{h}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}} . [LaTeX: N_{\text{s}}] N s N_{\text{s}} and [LaTeX: N_{\text{h}}] N h N_{\text{h}} denote the number of samples in each corresponding dataset. The Unified Push-Pull Objective. To achieve both robust safety and high utility, SOT integrates these two forces into a unified objective. We optimize [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}] 𝐰 \mathbf{w} to “pull” the distribution towards safety while simultaneously “pushing” it away from harm. We have the final objective formulated as: [LaTeX: \min_{\mathbf{w}}\big[(1\!-\!\lambda)\text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),Q)\!-\!\lambda\text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),M)\big],] min 𝐰 ⁡ [ ( − λ ) ​ OT ​ ( P ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) , Q ) − λ ​ OT ​ ( P ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) , M ) ] , \min_{\mathbf{w}}\big[(1\!-\!\lambda)\text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),Q)\!-\!\lambda\text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),M)\big], (5) where [LaTeX: \lambda\in[0,1]] λ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \lambda\in[0,1] controls the trade-off between safety alignment and harmful repulsion. By incorporating the OT distance, Eq. 5 reframes weight learning as a geometric transport problem, which evaluates a sample’s quality not by its isolated attributes, but by its transport cost relative to the entire safe manifold ( [LaTeX: Q] Q Q ) and harmful manifold ( [LaTeX: M] M M ). The Push force ( [LaTeX: \text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),M)] OT ​ ( P ​ ( 𝐰 ) , M ) \text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),M) ) acts as a discriminator, compressing the weights of samples that are semantically close to harmful samples (including camouflaged hard negatives) towards zero. The Pull force [LaTeX: \text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),Q)] OT ​ ( P ​ ( 𝐰 ) , Q ) \text{OT}(P(\mathbf{w}),Q) acts as a relevance ranker, ensuring that the remaining safe samples are weighted according to their semantic alignment with the task-specific anchor. To make Eq. 5 computationally tractable and differentiable, we adopt the Entropy-regularized Optimal Transport ( Cuturi, 2013 ) . The cost matrix (e.g., [LaTeX: \mathbf{C}^{s}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N_{c}\times N_{s}}] 𝐂 s ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 N c × N s \mathbf{C}^{s}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N_{c}\times N_{s}} between [LaTeX: P(\mathbf{w})] P ⁡ ( 𝐰 ) P(\mathbf{w}) and [LaTeX: Q] Q Q ) quantifies the semantic discrepancy using the Cosine Distance: [LaTeX: C_{ij}^{s}=1-\frac{\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}\|_{2}}.] C i ​ j s = 1 − 𝐳 i ⊤ ​ 𝐳 j ‖ 𝐳 i ‖ 2 ​ ‖ 𝐳 j ‖ 2 . C_{ij}^{s}=1-\frac{\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}\|_{2}}. For each sample pair, we construct the input context [Human: [LaTeX: x_{i}] x i x_{i} ; Assistant: [LaTeX: y_{i}] y i y_{i} ] and extract the the representation [LaTeX: \mathbf{z}_{i}] 𝐳 i \mathbf{z}_{i} from the frozen safety-aligned model [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} before the fine-tuning process. The transport plan (e.g., [LaTeX: \mathbf{T}^{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{c}\times N_{s}}_{\geq 0}] 𝐓 s ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 N c × N s \mathbf{T}^{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{c}\times N_{s}}_{\geq 0} ) should satisfy [LaTeX: \Pi(P(\mathbf{w}),Q):=\left\{\mathbf{T}^{s}\mid\sum_{i=1}^{N_{c}}T^{s}_{ij}=1/N_{s},\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}T^{s}_{ij}=w_{i}\right\}] Π ( P ( 𝐰 ) , Q ) := { 𝐓 s ∣ ∑ i = 1 N c T i ​ j s = 1 / N s , ∑ j = 1 N s T i ​ j s = w i } \Pi(P(\mathbf{w}),Q):=\left\{\mathbf{T}^{s}\mid\sum_{i=1}^{N_{c}}T^{s}_{ij}=1/N_{s},\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}T^{s}_{ij}=w_{i}\right\} . To optimize [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}] 𝐰 \mathbf{w} at each step, we first compute the optimal transport plans [LaTeX: \mathbf{T}^{s,*}] 𝐓 s , ∗ \mathbf{T}^{s,*} and [LaTeX: \mathbf{T}^{h,*}] 𝐓 h , ∗ \mathbf{T}^{h,*} by optimizing the corresponding entropy regularized OT loss, respectively. Since the optimal transport plans are the functions of [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}] 𝐰 \mathbf{w} , they are then utilized to compute the objective function [LaTeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{SOT}}] ℒ SOT \mathcal{L}_{\text{SOT}} . Finally, we update [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}] 𝐰 \mathbf{w} (parameterized via softmax) by minimizing the global Push-Pull objective [LaTeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{SOT}}] ℒ SOT \mathcal{L}_{\text{SOT}} via automatic differentiation using gradient descent. 4.2 Safety-Aware Fine-Tuning Hard Denoising via Top-K Selection. Given the optimized weight vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}^{*}] 𝐰 ∗ \mathbf{w}^{*} obtained by minimizing the final objective in Eq.( 6 ), low-quality samples in [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}_{\text{custom}}] 𝒟 custom \mathcal{D}_{\text{custom}} are naturally assigned lower weights, while higher weights correspond to more helpful and safer examples. Considering non-zero gradients from severe harmful samples might accumulate to degrade safety alignment, we apply a hard truncation strategy to filter out potentially toxic tails and improve training efficiency. We select the subset [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\text{custom}}] 𝒟 custom ′ \mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\text{custom}} corresponding to the Top- [LaTeX: K] K K indices of [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}^{*}] 𝐰 ∗ \mathbf{w}^{*} by: [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\text{custom}}\!=\!\left\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i},w^{\prime}_{i})^{\text{custom}}\mid i\in\text{Top-}K(\mathbf{w}^{*})\right\},] 𝒟 custom ′ = { ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 i , w i ′ ) custom ∣ i ∈ Top- ​ K ​ ( 𝐰 ∗ ) } , \mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\text{custom}}\!=\!\left\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i},w^{\prime}_{i})^{\text{custom}}\mid i\in\text{Top-}K(\mathbf{w}^{*})\right\}, (7) where [LaTeX: K] K K controls the size of the selected dataset, [LaTeX: \text{Top-}K(\mathbf{w}^{*})] Top- ​ K ​ ( 𝐰 ∗ ) \text{Top-}K(\mathbf{w}^{*}) denotes the set of indices corresponding to the [LaTeX: K] K K largest values in the learned weight vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}^{*}] 𝐰 ∗ \mathbf{w}^{*} . Within the selected safe subset, samples still vary in utility and relevance. We re-normalize the weights: [LaTeX: w^{\prime}_{i}=\frac{\exp(w_{i})}{\sum_{j\in\text{Top-}K(\mathbf{w}^{*})}\exp(w_{j})}] w i ′ = exp ⁡ ( w i ) ∑ j ∈ Top- ​ K ​ ( 𝐰 ∗ ) exp ⁡ ( w j ) w^{\prime}_{i}=\frac{\exp(w_{i})}{\sum_{j\in\text{Top-}K(\mathbf{w}^{*})}\exp(w_{j})} . \mathcal{L}_{\text{custom}}(\theta) in Eq.( 8 ). 11: end for Soft Emphasis via Weighted LLM Finetune. After constructing the Top- [LaTeX: K] K K subset [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\text{custom}}] 𝒟 custom ′ \mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{\text{custom}} and its corresponding weight vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}^{\prime}] 𝐰 ′ \mathbf{w}^{\prime} , we fine-tune the target LLM [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} by reweighting the standard supervised fine-tuning loss. Formally, the final training loss is defined as: [LaTeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{custom}}(\theta)\!=\!\!-\!\sum_{i=1}^{K}w^{\prime}_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{y}_{i}|}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{y}_{i}|}\,\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{ij}\!\mid\!\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i,<j}\bigr),] ℒ custom ( θ ) = − ∑ i = 1 K w i ′ ∑ j = 1 | 𝐲 i | 1 | 𝐲 i | log π θ ( y i ​ j ∣ 𝐱 i , y i , < j ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{custom}}(\theta)\!=\!\!-\!\sum_{i=1}^{K}w^{\prime}_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{y}_{i}|}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{y}_{i}|}\,\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{ij}\!\mid\!\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i,<j}\bigr), (8) where the re-normalized weight [LaTeX: w^{\prime}_{i}] w i ′ w^{\prime}_{i} acts as a safety coefficient, adaptively modulating the gradient magnitude for each sample, which ensures that the model updates are predominantly driven by high-utility, safety-aligned instances. Following Shen et al. (2025) , we employ LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) for efficient fine-tuning by injecting low-rank matrices while freezing the backbone, which effectively mitigates overfitting and integrates the safety-aligned sample weights. In summary, our framework introduces a systematic approach to data purification for safer SFT. By minimizing Optimal Transport distance in Eq.( 6 ) to optimize a sample-wise weight vector [LaTeX: \mathbf{w}] 𝐰 \mathbf{w} guided by reference distributions, we effectively redistribute the downstream dataset [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}_{\text{custom}}] 𝒟 custom \mathcal{D}_{\text{custom}} towards safety and helpfulness. As a benefit, not only does the learned vector provide a reliable criterion for filtering out low-quality data, but more importantly, it facilitates a weighted fine-tuning process that compels the model to prioritize high-quality, safe examples. Consequently, SOT achieves better alignment in both helpfulness and safety by strategically amplifying the learning signal from valuable data while mitigating the influence of harmful instances. We highlight our training process in Algorithm 1 .

Following Shen et al. (2025) ; Huang et al. (2024b) , we use SLIMORCA ( Lian et al., 2023 ) , MetaMathQA ( Yu et al., 2023 ) , AGNews ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) and the specialized legal dataset LegalBench-QA ( Menta, 2023 ) , which is derived from the original LegalBench benchmark ( Guha et al., 2023 ) as fine-tuning tasks. We use the red-team-attempts subset of HH dataset ( Bai et al., 2022 ) as the source of harmful data in the fine-tuning dataset. Within a fine-tuning dataset containing a total of [LaTeX: n] n n samples, we set the mixture of safe / harmful data as [LaTeX: 1-p\ :\ p] 1 − p : p 1-p\ :\ p , where the default setting is [LaTeX: p=0.1] p = 0.1 p=0.1 and [LaTeX: n=5000] n = 5000 n=5000 . For the harmful dataset, we employ a subset of 5,000 harmful samples from BeaverTails ( Ji et al., 2023 ) , while the safe dataset comprises 50 samples from the corresponding custom downstream dataset. Experimental setting. For SOT, we set [LaTeX: \lambda] λ \lambda as 0.5 and fix [LaTeX: \epsilon=0.1] ϵ = 0.1 \epsilon=0.1 in computing the transport plan. We extract the last-token hidden state in the last layer from the frozen safety-aligned model [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} as the representation [LaTeX: \mathbf{z}] 𝐳 \mathbf{z} . For a fair comparison, we select 80% data (i.e., [LaTeX: K=4000] K = 4000 K=4000 ) as the fine-tuning data following Shen et al. (2025) . We adopt LoRA for accelerating the LLM fine-tuning and train [LaTeX: \pi_{\theta}] π θ \pi_{\theta} for 2 epochs. Detailed hyper-parameters and setups can be found in Appendix A.1 and Appendix A.2 . Baselines. To fairly prove the effectiveness of our method, we consider the following baselines: 1) Standard SFT. 2) Data Selection Methods, including random selection, ALPAGASUS ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and DSIR ( Xie et al., 2023 ) . 3) Safety Fine-tuning Methods based on Data Selection and Reweighting, including SAFT ( Choi et al., 2024 ) , BDS ( Hu et al., 2025 ) and SEAL ( Shen et al., 2025 ) . 4) Structure-Aware Methods and Instruction Fine-Tuning Methods, including Salora ( Li et al., 2025b ) and SafeInstr ( Bianchi et al., 2024 ) . More details of these baselines are in Appendix A.3 . Models and Evaluation. Following Shen et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) , we evaluate the effectiveness of SOT on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) , Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) , Qwen3-8B ( Team, 2025b ) , and gemma-3-4b-it ( Team, 2025a ) . We construct a Helpfulness test set and a Harmfulness test set to evaluate the fine-tuned LLM, both including 1000 samples from the corresponding downstream task datasets and red-team-attempts dataset. We define Helpfulness Score (HpS) and Harmfulness Score (HmS) to assess the performance and safety of fine-tuned LLM by adopting a popular LLM-as-a-judgment evaluation strategy. For the AGNews dataset, we use Accuracy (Acc.) to measure the model’s classification performance. Finally, we use Average Score (Avg.) to measure the overall performance of the model in terms of safety and usefulness. More details can be found in Appendix A.4 . 5.2 Main Results Experimental Results. Tab. 1 shows that SOT consistently achieves significant performance improvement across both Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-3-8B families, demonstrating robust generalization capabilities. Specifically, SOT yields the highest Avg. across all evaluated datasets, including SLIMORCA, AGNews, MetaMathQA, and GSM8K. Critically, SOT attains the lowest HmS in every scenario, significantly outperforming competitive baselines like DSIR and SEAL in safety alignment. While standard SFT or ALPAGASUS occasionally achieve high utility scores (e.g., accuracy on AGNews or HpS on MetaMathQA), they often do so at a substantial cost to safety. In contrast, SOT maintains highly competitive and often superior HpS, effectively navigating the safety-utility tradeoff. This universal improvement across diverse downstream domains and distinct model architectures underscores SOT’s efficacy as a balanced and scalable solution for real-world LLM usage. In addition, we provide results on Llama3-8B-Instruct and Gemma3-4B-it in Appendix A.5 , where we find the consistently improved performance compared with strong baselines. Specialized Domain Generalization on Law. Beyond general benchmarks, SOT demonstrates exceptional efficacy in specialized domains, as evidenced by results on the LegalBench-QA dataset. As shown in Tab. 2 , SOT achieves a better safety-utility trade-off, securing the highest average score (0.834) while maintaining a significantly lower harmfulness score (0.105) compared to all tuned baselines. Notably, while competitive methods like DSIR may achieve higher Helpfulness Scores, they often incur much higher safety risks. SOT’s ability to substantially improve safety with minimal impact on utility in a high-stakes legal context highlights its practical robustness and adaptability across both general and specific domains. Tab. 3 presents a holistic ablation study examining the individual contributions of SOT’s components—specifically its objectives and fine-tuning strategies—alongside the reference data sources. (1) First and foremost, the results demonstrate that the “Pull” and “Push” objectives are mutually indispensable. While the “Pull Only” configuration (HmS: 0.224) establishes a baseline for safety convergence, and “Push Only” (HmS: 0.441) struggles without a constructive target, the superior safety-utility trade-off is achieved only when both forces are combined (HmS: 0.197). This confirms that neither mechanism is sufficient in isolation: the “Pull” force provides the necessary guidance towards the safe manifold, while the “Push” force serves as an essential negative constraint to actively purify adversarial spaces that a positive reference alone cannot address. (2) Beyond the learning objective, our analysis of the fine-tuning strategy reveals a strong synergy between filtering and reweighting. While the “Top-K Only” approach effectively acts as a hard denoiser to truncate toxic long-tail samples (HmS: 0.205), it is the integration with “Reweighting"—which offers a smoother optimization landscape—that allows the full SOT strategy to maximize the Average Score. This combined approach ensures that while the most harmful instances are removed, the remaining safe subset is further refined by up-weighting high-quality samples. (3) Finally, the study highlights the distinct nature of our distribution matching dependencies. We find that for the “Pull” mechanism, replacing the task-specific safe anchor with a general safe dataset (e.g., BeaverTails) leads to a sharp degradation in safety. In contrast, the “Push” mechanism demonstrates remarkable robustness: substituting the default harmful reference with an alternative harmful dataset maintains comparable. This indicates that while the guidance towards safety must be precise and task-aligned, the repulsion from harmfulness generalizes effectively across different manifestations of toxicity. Impact of Selection and Harmful Ratios. As illustrated in Fig. 2 (Left), SOT maintains a robust Average Score (Avg.) of approximately 0.8 across selection rates ranging from 10% to 90%, consistently surpassing SEAL and SFT. Notably, the performance gap widens as the selection rate decreases; this validates that SOT excels at prioritizing the highest-quality samples, ensuring superior alignment even with a minimal data budget. The framework’s resilience to data contamination is further evidenced in Fig. 2 (Middle). While baselines suffer precipitous degradation as the harmful ratio [LaTeX: p] p p increases, SOT sustains a stable profile near 0.8, even under severe contamination. Crucially, SOT outperforms standard SFT even in pristine regimes ( [LaTeX: p=0] p = 0 p=0 ), highlighting its ability to amplify high-utility samples through safety-aware reweighting independent of noise removal. This stability across the spectrum demonstrates SOT’s dual capacity for precise data identification and robust learning in adversarial scenarios. Data Efficiency and Asymmetry. Fig. 2 (Right) reveals a distinct asymmetry in reference data requirements. The rapid saturation of the blue curve demonstrates that the safe anchor provides directional guidance, achieving near-optimal performance with as few as [LaTeX: N_{\text{safe}}\in[10,50]] N safe ∈ [ 10 , 50 ] N_{\text{safe}}\in[10,50] samples. In contrast, the “Push” mechanism (red curve) exhibits a scale dependence, reflecting the volumetric necessity of covering the diverse, high-variance manifold of toxicity. Despite these differing demands, SOT consistently outperforms baselines (SEAL and SFT) across all settings. This confirms that SOT efficiently anchors safety with minimal clean demonstrations while leveraging broad negative coverage to fortify the adversarial boundary. Figure 3: Distribution of Learned Weights using Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on the SLIMORCA dataset. Visualization of Learned Weight. Fig. 3 shows the weight distributions learned for harmful and safe samples across the three methods. While “Pull Only” correctly identifies safe samples, it fails to suppress harmful ones, resulting in a distributional overlap. Conversely, “Push Only” lacks a constructive anchor, struggling to establish clear separation boundaries. In contrast, SOT effectively disentangles these distributions by concentrating high weights on safe samples while reducing the weight distribution of harmful samples. This confirms that the dual “push-pull” mechanism is essential for robustly reshaping the weight landscape. We visualize the sample-level weight in Fig. 6 in Appendix A.10 . Additional Results. We validate the robust filtering performance (Appendix A.7 ) and stability across hyperparameters including [LaTeX: \lambda] λ \lambda (Appendix A.8 ) and representation layers (Appendix A.9 ). sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.text: 7 Limitations While our proposed Safety Optimal Transport (SOT) framework demonstrates significant improvements in balancing safety and utility during fine-tuning, several limitations remain: 1. Dependence on Quality of Reference Datasets: The effectiveness of the SOT framework is intrinsically linked to the quality and representativeness of the reference datasets ( [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}_{safe}] 𝒟 s ​ a ​ f ​ e \mathcal{D}_{safe} and [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}_{harmful}] 𝒟 h ​ a ​ r ​ m ​ f ​ u ​ l \mathcal{D}_{harmful} ). If the safe reference distribution is biased or if the harmful reference dataset fails to cover specific types of toxicity, the computed transport weights may not accurately reflect the true safety quality of the downstream samples. 2. Adapting to Evolving Adversarial Patterns: SOT effectively mitigates risks represented by harmful reference datasets [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}_{harmful}] 𝒟 h ​ a ​ r ​ m ​ f ​ u ​ l \mathcal{D}_{harmful} . However, adversarial attack strategies targeting large language models are rapidly evolving (e.g., multilingual jailbreak attacks or cryptographic attacks). Current frameworks assume reference distributions are static; maintaining robustness against future unknown attack vectors theoretically requires updates to reference datasets to cover these emerging patterns. 3. Interpretability of Transport Decisions: While the SOT can provide quantitative weights [LaTeX: w^{*}] w ∗ w^{*} for each sample, it currently cannot generate natural language explanations for why specific samples are prioritized or penalized. While the visualizations in Appendix A.10 offer statistical insights, developing more intuitive, human-readable interfaces to track specific “push” or “pull” decisions remains a valuable avenue for enhancing safety alignment transparency. 4. Evaluation Proxy Bias: Our evaluation metrics, specifically the Helpfulness Score (HpS) and Harmfulness Score (HmS), rely on LLM-as-a-judge methodologies. While this is a standard practice in recent literature, LLM judges may harbor inherent biases or discrepancies compared to human evaluation, potentially affecting the granularity of safety assessments.
